newsitem.title: PERU: Families mourn slain Peru commandos, hostage.
newsitem.headline: Families mourn slain Peru commandos, hostage.

text.p: Gazing at dusty hills overlooking the cemetery, Emilsa Chavez wept on Thursday as she remembered her soldier son whom she had not seen for four months and whose body now lay before her in a coffin draped with the Peruvian flag.

Two days earlier she received news that her son, army Lt. Raul Jimenez, had died in a hail of gunfire during a spectacular assault to free hostages held by guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence.
"I never would have imagined that these sorts of things happened. It came as a complete surprise," said Chavez, her voice breaking with emotion as she leant on her husband's arm for support.
Chavez, dressed in black, sobbed quietly as Peru's armed forces buried Jimenez and the only other commando killed in the raid, Col. Juan Valer, as national heroes side-by-side.

She had not seen her son, 27, since December when all home leave was suddenly banned as elite commandos began assiduous training for the explosive storming of the diplomatic compound taken by Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels.
"I miss him. He was very caring with all his family, especially with me," she said.

Jimenez's fiancee, Claudia Barrantes, cried inconsolably as the red-and-white flags were dragged off the metal coffins that were then opened to allow the families to look on their loved ones for the last time.
Relatives, including Valer's 10-year-old daughter, Valeria, dropped white flowers into the graves after the coffins had been lowered into the ground.
The only hostage killed in the attack, Supreme Court judge Carlos Giusti, was buried in a private service later in the day just a few hundred yards from the slain commandos.
Giusti bled to death after being shot in the fierce 40- minute gun-battle in which all 14 Marxist rebels were killed.

Joined in the sweltering heat by hundreds of uniformed soldiers and scores of the men's families and friends, President Alberto Fujimori watched grimly as tributes were read by military colleagues to the two soldiers.
Standing behind him with tears constantly sliding down his cheeks, was Fujimori's 16-year old son Kenji, for whom Valer had served as bodyguard.
Seven bullets killed Valer as he led Foreign Minister Franciso Tudela, the rebels' prize captive, to safety across the roof of the diplomatic residence.
"He was a very brave man. He was a commando prepared for death and to sacrifice himself to save others," said Felipe Elias, Valer's brother-in-law, after the service.
"I don't think he would have wanted to die in any other way."
His voice quaking with emotion, one of Valer's colleagues read out a farewell letter the 38-year old soldier had written to his men in which he sensed he might not survive the assault.
"Think that I am at peace and the only thing that I want is that people say Valer was a good man," it said.
